Data science is being applied right now in every industry you can name. These examples are drawn from real applications - the same techniques you will learn in this course power each of them.
Player Evaluation & Scouting

MLB teams use pandas and statistical modeling to evaluate prospects from minor league data. The Moneyball revolution (Oakland A's, 2002) showed that data could find market inefficiencies in player valuation. Today every major team employs data scientists.

Machine learning models trained on medical imaging data can detect diabetic retinopathy, lung cancer, and skin lesions with accuracy matching or exceeding specialist physicians. NumPy and Python underpin the entire image processing pipeline.

Credit card companies process billions of transactions daily, flagging potentially fraudulent ones in real time using anomaly detection models. The pandas cleaning and feature engineering you will learn in Module 4 is the foundation of this pipeline.

"Customers who bought X also bought Y." These systems are trained on purchase history matrices using collaborative filtering - a technique built on NumPy array operations. A widely cited McKinsey analysis put the share of Amazon purchases driven by recommendations at around 35%.

Climate scientists use Python (NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib) to process satellite data, model atmospheric conditions, and communicate findings. The visualizations you see in IPCC reports are generated with the tools from Module 5.
Predictive Policing & Bias Detection

Government agencies use data science for resource allocation, but the field also grapples with ethical failures - biased training data producing discriminatory models. Critical thinking (Module 1) is as important as technical skill.

Data science is the practice of extracting knowledge and insight from data through a combination of statistics, programming, and domain expertise. The oft-cited "Venn diagram" definition says data science sits at the intersection of three areas: math and statistics , computer science and programming , and domain knowledge . You need at least two of the three to be effective, and all three to be exceptional.

A more practical definition: data scientists build systems that turn raw data into decisions. Those decisions might be automated (a recommendation engine, a fraud detection model) or human-assisted (a dashboard that helps an executive understand churn). Either way, the job is to move from messy, ambiguous data toward a clear, defensible answer.
Data science vs. data engineering vs. ML engineering

The field has fragmented into specializations. Data scientists build models and generate insight. Data engineers build the pipelines that move and store data at scale. ML engineers take a data scientist's prototype model and deploy it into production systems. In a small company, one person often does all three; at large companies they are distinct teams.
Data Science vs. Data Analytics
These two terms are often used interchangeably, but they have a meaningful distinction. Understanding the difference helps you know what kind of work you are being asked to do.

Python has become the dominant language of data science. It is a general-purpose language designed not specifically for data science, but a combination of factors made it the community standard.

Readable syntax. Python reads almost like English pseudocode. A data scientist can spend their cognitive load on the problem rather than the syntax (the code). Compare writing a loop in Python vs. Java and the difference is immediately apparent.

The ecosystem. NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, scikit-learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch - all Python-first. The open-source community has built a set of libraries for every step of the data pipeline. This creates a network effect in which people use Python because the libraries are there; the libraries improve because people use Python. Other languages, like R, have similar communities.

Glue language. Python can call code written in C, Fortran, R, and Java. The heavy numerical computation in NumPy is actually running C code under the hood. You get ease of use at the surface and raw speed where it counts.

Community and employers. The majority of job postings for data science roles list Python as a required or preferred skill. Choosing Python means choosing the largest community and largest community resources.

The truth about coding languages. In reality, once you learn one language, you will be able to use the others easily. The most important part of coding isn't the code itself, but understanding the thinking process involved in solving problems with code.

R is Python's main competitor in academic and statistical contexts. R was designed by statisticians for statistical computing and is excellent for certain tasks, particularly advanced statistical modeling and publication-quality plots. But Python is ahead of R in industry because of its broader applicability. If you go into academic research or biostatistics, you may need R. For most industry data science roles, Pyth
Critical Thinking for Data Scientists

Technical skills are necessary but not sufficient. A data scientist who cannot think critically about a problem will build the wrong model correctly - which is worse than building nothing at all. These mental habits separate effective practitioners from technically competent ones.
Ask the right question first

Most projects fail not because of poor modeling but because the question was never precisely stated. "How do we improve sales?" is not an answerable data science question. "Which customer segments have the highest 90-day churn rate, and what behaviors predict churn 30 days in advance?" is. Before touching data, you should be able to state: what decision will this analysis inform, and what would a good answer look lik
Correlation is not causation

This is the most-repeated phrase in statistics for a reason. Finding that two variables move together does not tell you why. Ice cream sales and drowning rates are correlated - because both increase in summer. Acting on that correlation would be absurd. Whenever you find a relationship in data, ask: what third variable could explain this? Could the causality run the other direction? Is this a coincidence in a small s
Know your data's provenance

Before analyzing data, understand how it was collected. Surveys have response bias. Clickstream data reflects only users who stayed on the page. Hospital admission data does not represent the general population. Every dataset has selection effects baked in. Ignoring them leads to confident, wrong conclusions.
Uncertainty is not failure

A good data scientist quantifies uncertainty and communicates it clearly. Saying "we are 80% confident that treatment B outperforms treatment A by 5-15%" is more honest and more useful than saying "B is better than A." Decision-makers need to know the confidence interval, not just the point estimate.
A 6-Step Problem-Solving Framework

Before writing a single line of Python, effective data scientists work through the problem systematically. This six-step framework builds the habit of thinking before coding - which saves far more time than it costs.
Comprehend requirements and constraints. Identify the inputs, outputs, and any specific rules or conditions that must be met.
Consider the logical flow. Make a general outline of the major steps. Think about which data structures or algorithms might be suitable.
Divide the plan into smaller, more manageable sub-problems. Each sub-problem should be solvable independently.
Write a human-friendly description of what the program should do - without worrying about Python syntax yet.
Implement each sub-problem in Python. You don't always have to start at the beginning - tackle the parts you understand first.
Check that your solution works on expected inputs and edge cases. Learn to read error messages as instructions, not failures.
Pseudocode: Thinking Before Coding

Pseudocode is a structured plain-language description of an algorithm - formal enough to be unambiguous, but free of any specific programming language syntax. It forces you to think through the logic of a solution before you are distracted by syntax errors and edge cases.
Good data scientists write pseudocode before they open a Jupyter notebook. It is faster to iterate on an idea in plain language than to debug Python that implements the wrong algorithm.

Problem: Given a roster of players with batting averages, identify the player with the highest average who has played at least 20 games.

Every value in Python has a type , and the type determines what you're allowed to do with the value. Getting types wrong is probably the single most common source of errors in data work, so it's worth being deliberate here.
The type function tells you what you've got.

The quotes are what make something a string. 42 is a number; '42' is text that happens to look like a number. Python treats them very differently.

Naming things well is most of what makes code readable.

Notice: no output . This is an assignment statement , and a statement performs an action rather than producing a value. It has three parts - the variable name on the left, the = assignment operator , and an expression on the right.

A variable's value can change. Assign to the same name again and the old value is simply gone.
attempts = 1 attempts = 2 attempts

This is worth pausing on, because the = sign is misleading. In mathematics, = asserts that two things are equal. In Python, = is an instruction: take the value on the right and store it under the name on the left . It's an action, not a claim.
Which is why this works, and would be nonsense in algebra:
count = 5 count = count + 3 count
8 . Python evaluates the right side first - count + 3 is 5 + 3 , or 8 - and then stores that result back under the name count . The old value of 5 is overwritten in the process.
Read = as "gets" rather than "equals" and this stops being confusing: count gets count + 3 .
Adding to a variable is common enough that Python has a shorthand. These two lines do the same thing:
count = count + 3 count += 3
count = 5 count += 3 count
You'll see += constantly once we get to loops, where it's how you accumulate a running total.
Names can contain letters, digits, and underscores, but they cannot start with a digit and cannot contain spaces or punctuation. Break those rules and you get a SyntaxError.

The empty parentheses () mean this function takes no inputs.
The first line is the header and it must end with a colon.
The indented lines below are the body .

Indentation is syntax in Python. In most languages, indenting is a courtesy to readers; in Python it's how the language knows which lines belong to the function. Four spaces is the universal convention. Be consistent - mixing tabs and spaces produces errors that are genuinely hard to see.
Now call it. Parentheses are what trigger the call:
Not the output - a description of the function object itself.

Without parentheses you're referring to the function as a value , the same way gpa refers to a number. With parentheses you're telling Python to run it. This distinction shows up again in Module 4, where you hand functions to pandas as arguments without calling them.
A function that always does the same thing has limited use. A parameter is a variable in the header that receives a value when the function is called.
def print_heading (text): print (text) print ( "=" * len (text))

One definition, different output each time.
Two words that get used loosely and shouldn't be:

an argument is the actual value you pass in ( "Cohort Summary" )
The parameter is the slot; the argument is what you put in it. Error messages use both words precisely, so it pays to know which is which.
You can pass a variable as the argument - the value gets handed over, and the parameter name inside the function is unrelated to the variable name outside:

Give the wrong number of arguments and you get a TypeError , with a message that names the function and counts the arguments for you:

Return values - the important distinction
This is the concept students most often get halfway. Take it slowly.
print puts text on the screen for a human to read. return hands a value back to the program so it can be used. They are not alternatives to each other; they do different jobs.
Here is a function that prints:
def show_letter_grade (gpa): if gpa >= 3.5 : print ( "A" ) else : print ( "B or below" )
show_letter_grade ( 3.81 )
Looks like it works. Now try to use the result:
result = show_letter_grade ( 3.81 ) print ( f"result is {result}, of type {type(result)}" )

The function printed "A" as a side effect, then ended without returning anything - and a function that returns nothing returns None , a special value meaning "no value at all." The text went to the screen, where you can read it but your program can't.
None showing up unexpectedly almost always means this: a function printed when it should have returned.
Same logic, with return :
def letter_grade (gpa): if gpa >= 3.5 : return "A" else : return "B or below"
result = letter_grade ( 3.81 ) print ( f"result is {result!r}, of type {type(result)}" )
Now the value is in your hands. You can store it, test it, put it in an f-string, or feed it to another function:
print_heading ( letter_grade ( 3.81 ))

Rule of thumb: functions should return, not print. A function that returns can always be printed by whoever calls it. A function that prints can never be un-printed. Printing is a decision about presentation, and it belongs at the edge of your program, not buried in the middle of it.
You will violate this rule sometimes - print_heading above prints, and that's fine because presentation is literally its job. The point is to violate it on purpose.
One more thing about return : it ends the function immediately. Anything after it never runs.
def area (radius): return 3.14159 * radius ** 2 print ( "Hello, World!" ) area ( 3 )
No printed message - return exited before reaching it. Unreachable code after a return is a common symptom of a half-finished edit.
Variables created inside a function are local : they exist while the function runs and then they're gone.
def normalized_engagement (logins, hours): login_score = logins / 20 hour_score = hours / 15 return (login_score + hour_score) / 2 normalized_engagement ( 14 , 9.5 )

login_score was never visible outside the function. This is a feature: you can write a function without worrying about whether one of its variable names collides with something elsewhere in a 200-line notebook.

A docstring is a string on the first line of a function body that says what the function does. help() displays it. You will read docstrings constantly in NumPy and pandas; write one for anything you'll use more than once.

A boolean expression evaluates to True or False . The == operator asks whether two values are equal.
bool is a type with exactly two values, True and False . Capitalized, no quotes - true is a NameError and 'True' is a string.
** = and == are different operators and confusing them is a rite of passage.** = assigns a value. == compares two values. Using = where a comparison belongs is a SyntaxError:
gpa = 3.81 if gpa = 3.5 : print ( 'yes' )
Python's message here is unusually kind: "Maybe you meant '==' or ':=' instead of '='?" Ignore the := suggestion for now.
The full set of relational operators :

gpa = 3.81 cutoff = 3.5 print (gpa == cutoff) # equal to print (gpa != cutoff) # not equal to print (gpa > cutoff) # greater than print (gpa < cutoff) # less than print (gpa >= cutoff) # greater than or equal to print (gpa <= cutoff) # less than or equal to
Three operators combine boolean expressions: and , or , not .
and is True only if both sides are True :
gpa = 3.81 credits = 124 gpa >= 3.5 and credits >= 120
or is True if either side is (or both):
gpa >= 3.9 or credits >= 120
gpa >= 3.9 and credits >= 120 or gpa >= 3.5
True - but if you had to think hard about why , that's the lesson.
and binds more tightly than or , so Python reads it as (gpa >= 3.9 and credits >= 120) or (gpa >= 3.5) . The first group is False , the second is True , so the or is True .
Correct, and unreadable. Add the parentheses even when you don't need them - the next person to read this, including you, shouldn't have to remember an operator precedence table.
The if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is true. The structure is the same shape as a function definition: header ending in a colon, indented body.
gpa = 3.81 if gpa >= 3.5 : print ( "Dean's list" )
Change the value and the block is skipped entirely - no output, no error:
gpa = 2.94 if gpa >= 3.5 : print ( "Dean's list" )
else supplies the alternative:
gpa = 2.94 if gpa >= 3.5 : print ( "Dean's list" ) else : print ( "Not on the Dean's list" )
Exactly one of those two branches runs, always. The if and the else are two paths through the same fork.
Real classification has more than two outcomes, and elif - short for "else if" - handles the middle cases.

def standing (gpa): """Return a student's academic standing from their GPA.""" if gpa >= 3.5 : return "excellent" elif gpa >= 3.0 : return "good" elif gpa >= 2.0 : return "satisfactory" else : return "at risk" print ( standing ( 3.81 )) print ( standing ( 3.02 )) print ( standing ( 2.60 )) print ( standing ( 1.90 ))

You can have as many elif branches as you need, and the else is optional. Python checks the conditions top to bottom and stops at the first one that's true - which is why the order matters enormously.
Notice standing(3.81) returns "excellent" even though 3.81 >= 3.0 is also true. The first match wins and the rest are never evaluated.
Two functions, one difference that matters
These two functions look nearly identical. They behave completely differently. This is the most important cell in the section.

def standing_elif (gpa): if gpa >= 3.5 : return "excellent" elif gpa >= 3.0 : return "good" elif gpa >= 2.0 : return "satisfactory" else : return "at risk" def standing_if (gpa): if gpa >= 3.5 : print ( "excellent" ) if gpa >= 3.0 : print ( "good" ) if gpa >= 2.0 : print ( "satisfactory" ) else : print ( "at risk" )
print ( "--- elif version ---" ) print ( standing_elif ( 3.81 )) print ( "--- if version ---" ) standing_if ( 3.81 )
The if version prints three lines: excellent , good , and satisfactory .

Separate if statements are independent questions. Python asks all three, and 3.81 satisfies all three, so all three bodies run. A chain of elif is one question with several possible answers - at most one body runs.

Worse, look at that else . It's attached only to the last if , so it fires whenever gpa < 2.0 , regardless of the earlier branches. Try standing_if(1.5) and you'll get at risk alone, which happens to be right. Try it on a value where the branches disagree and the logic falls apart.
**When your conditions are mutually exclusive alternatives, you want elif .** Separate if statements are for genuinely independent checks.

Here's where lists differ from strings in a way that matters. Strings are immutable - no method changes one in place. Lists are mutable: you can assign to a position and change the list itself.
scores = [ 88 , 92 , 79 ] scores[ 0 ] = 95 scores
Try the equivalent on a string:

That TypeError - 'str' object does not support item assignment - is Python saying strings are immutable. .append() adds one element to the end. Note that it modifies the list in place and returns nothing:
scores = [ 88 , 92 , 79 ] scores. append ( 93 ) scores

scores. extend ([ 85 , 91 ]) scores
Now the contrast that catches everyone. What if you append a list instead of extending?

.append() adds one element, and that one element happens to itself be a list. You get a nested list: six numbers and then a list sitting in position
Look at the output and you can see the inner brackets.

.pop() removes an element by position and returns it; .remove() deletes by value:
letters = [ 'a' , 'b' , 'c' , 'd' ] removed = letters. pop ( 1 ) letters. remove ( 'c' ) print ( f"removed {removed!r}, list is now {letters}" )
The in operator asks whether a value appears in a list. It returns a boolean, so it drops straight into an if .
Four built-in functions do most of what you'll want. sum , min , max , and len - and with those four you can compute a mean.
print ( f"sum: {sum(ug_gpas)}" ) print ( f"min: {min(ug_gpas)}" ) print ( f"max: {max(ug_gpas)}" ) print ( f"mean: {sum(ug_gpas) / len(ug_gpas):.3f}" )
sorted returns a new list in order and leaves the original alone; reverse=True sorts high to low. It sorts strings too, alphabetically.
print ( sorted (ug_gpas, reverse= True )[: 3 ]) # top three print (ug_gpas) # unchanged

scores = [ 88 , 92 , 79 ] backup = scores # a second name, not a copy real_copy = list (scores) # an independent copy scores. append ( 999 ) print ( f"backup: {backup}" ) print ( f"real_copy: {real_copy}" )

A dictionary is a mapping
A list maps positions to values - index 0 gets you the first element. A dictionary maps keys to values , and the keys can be anything you like.

No searching, no position tracking. And unlike parallel lists, the pairing can't come apart.

The anatomy of a for loop
for raw in roster: print ( clean_name (raw))
for and in are keywords. The header ends with a colon; the body is indented.
raw is the loop variable . You choose the name.
roster is the sequence being iterated over.

What happens when it runs: raw is assigned the first element and the body executes. Then raw is assigned the second element and the body executes again. And so on until the sequence is exhausted, at which point the loop ends and Python moves to the next line after the body.
The loop variable name is yours to pick and the loop doesn't care what it is:
for cheeseburger in [ "a" , "b" , "c" ]: print (cheeseburger)
It works, and please don't. Name the loop variable after one element of what you're looping over - for raw in roster , for gpa in ug_gpas , for student in cohort . The name is documentation.
The sequence name, on the other hand, has to be real:
for name in rooster: print (name)
A NameError and a typo. Read the name in the message - rooster - and the fix is obvious. Most NameErrors are misspellings.
You also can't loop over something that isn't a sequence:
'int' object is not iterable - a single number isn't a collection of things. If you wanted the numbers 0 through 9, that's what range is for.

for i in range ( 5 ): print (i)
Note it starts at 0 and stops before 5 - the same exclusive-stop convention as slicing. range(5) gives you five numbers, which is usually what you want. You can also give a start and a step:

A detour: tuples, and unpacking
What enumerate actually hands back on each pass is a single value containing two things - a tuple .
# What one item from enumerate looks like on its own item = list ( enumerate ([ "a" , "b" ]))[ 0 ] print (item) print ( type (item))
A tuple is an ordered collection, written with parentheses and commas. It is very nearly a list, with one important difference: a tuple is immutable. Once built, it cannot be changed.
pair = ( 0 , "Amaka Okoroha" ) print (pair[ 0 ]) # index it like a list print (pair[ 1 ]) print ( len (pair))
Same does not support item assignment message you saw when trying to modify a string, and for the same reason - strings and tuples are both immutable, lists and dictionaries are not.
Unpacking is what lets you pull a tuple apart into separate names in one step:
index, name = pair # unpack two values into two names print (index) print (name)

That is exactly what for i, raw in enumerate(roster) is doing on every pass through the loop. It's also how you'll take two values back from a function later, and how you'll loop over a dictionary in section 6.

You do not need to build tuples yourself in this course. You do need to recognize one when you see it, because Python hands them back constantly - and because the error message when you try to modify one is otherwise baffling.
enumerate pairs each element with its position. When two lists are in the same order, zip pairs them with each other , one element from each on every pass:
for raw, gpa in zip (roster, ug_gpas): print ( f"{clean_name(raw):20} {gpa:.2f}" )
Each pass hands back a tuple, unpacked into two names exactly as with enumerate . One thing to know: zip stops at the end of the shorter list, silently.
print ( list ( zip ([ 1 , 2 , 3 ], [ "a" , "b" ])))
The 3 simply disappears, with no error. If two lists are supposed to line up, check that their lengths match before you zip them. You'll see zip again in Modules 3 and 5.
Here is the single most important loop pattern in data work. You want a total, so you start at zero and add to a variable each time through.
total = 0 for gpa in ug_gpas: total += gpa print ( f"total: {total}" ) print ( f"mean: {total / len(ug_gpas):.3f}" )
Three parts, and every accumulator has them:
Initialize before the loop - total = 0 .
Update inside the loop - total += gpa .
Use after the loop - the mean.
Getting the initialization inside the loop by accident is a classic bug: total would reset to zero every iteration and you'd end up with just the last value.

This is the most common way data cleaning fails: the code runs happily, raises nothing, and leaves the problem in place. Had we not printed the values and looked at them, this would have traveled all the way into the Cabinet's report.
The fix is a small idiom worth memorizing. .split() breaks the string on any run of whitespace and discards the empties; " ".join(...) puts it back together with exactly one space between pieces:

""" return " " . join (raw. split ()). title () clean_roster = [] for raw in roster: clean_roster. append ( clean_name (raw)) for name in clean_roster: print ( f"[{name}]" )

Real name handling is genuinely hard and no one-line fix exists. .title() is fine for this cohort. On real data you would check the output against the source, which is the same lesson as above: look at your values.

Three loop hazards, all worth remembering.

A word about how this feels

Programmers make mistakes constantly. The mistakes are called bugs and finding them is debugging , and if you're new to this, the volume of errors can feel like evidence that you're bad at it. It isn't. Experienced programmers generate errors at a similar rate; they just recognize them faster and panic less.

One framing that helps: think of the computer as an employee with unusual strengths - enormous speed, perfect precision, total consistency - and unusual weaknesses - no judgment, no context, no ability to guess what you meant. Your job is to be a good manager of that employee. When it does something absurd, it is following your instructions exactly. The instructions were the problem, and the error message is the empl

Frustration is normal and it's also expensive, because it makes you skip the step where you actually read the message. Almost every error message tells you what went wrong and where. Read it before you change anything.

A notebook is not a script. Cells run when you run them, and they all share the same namespace. Which means the notebook you're looking at may not reflect the state Python is actually in.

The factorial of $n$ is $n \times (n-1) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1$. So $5! = 5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$.

def factorial (n): """Return n factorial, the product of all integers from 1 to n.""" result = 1 # 1, not 0 -- multiplying by 0 zeroes it out for i in range ( 1 , n + 1 ): result *= i return result for n in [ 0 , 1 , 5 , 10 ]: print ( f"{n:3}! = {factorial(n)}" )

The accumulator's starting value depends on the operation. For a sum you start at 0 ; for a product you must start at 1 , because anything multiplied by zero is zero and you would get 0 every time. The identity value for the operation is the right starting point.

** range(1, n + 1) needs that + 1 .** range excludes its stop value, so range(1, n) would stop one short and quietly give you the wrong answer. Off-by-one errors live in exactly this spot - whenever you write a range with two arguments, check the last value it actually produces.

Programming has a precise vocabulary, and using it precisely is important - it's what lets you ask for or search for help and get an answer. When you can write "TypeError when concatenating str and int" instead of "my code is broken," your instructor, GAs, and the internet become useful to you.
Learning these is like learning addition and subtraction in math - you'll use them in everything you do going forward.
operator - A symbol that performs a computation: + , - , ** , % , // . What it does depends on the types either side of it.
expression - Anything Python can evaluate down to a single value. 2 + 2 , len(name) , and 3.81 are all expressions.
value - One piece of data: a number, a string, a list. Everything in Python is a value of some type.
type - The kind of thing a value is - int , float , str , bool , list , dict . Determines which operations are legal on it.
statement - A line that does something rather than producing a value. An assignment, an if , a for , an import .
assignment - Binding a name to a value with = . The name is a label, not a box: two names can label the same object.
keyword - A word reserved by the language - if , for , def , return , None . You cannot use one as a variable name.
function - A named block of code you can run on demand, optionally taking inputs and handing back a result.
argument - The actual value you pass in when you call a function. print("hi") passes the argument "hi" .
parameter - The name in a function's definition that receives an argument. The parameter is the slot; the argument is what goes in it.
return value - What a function hands back to the code that called it. A function that only prints returns None .
local variable - A name created inside a function. It exists while the function runs and is gone afterwards.
method - A function that belongs to an object and is called with a dot: name.strip() , scores.append(3) .
module - A file of Python code you can import and use. numpy and pandas are modules other people wrote.
sequence - An ordered collection you can index and iterate: a list, a string, a tuple.
index - The position of an item in a sequence, counting from zero . roster[0] is the first name.
slice - A range taken from a sequence, start:stop , where stop is excluded . xs[1:3] gives two items.

NumPy stores its numbers in a compact C format, not as Python objects. Every time a Python loop pulls one out, NumPy has to manufacture a Python object to hand over - and then throw it away on the next iteration. Two hundred thousand values means two hundred thousand pointless object creations, on top of the loop overhead the list version already pays.

Now look at those two speedup numbers again. Both are real measurements of real code. Only one is a fair comparison, because the larger figure is measuring vectorization plus a self-inflicted penalty that has nothing to do with vectorization.

The honest claim is the smaller one: vectorizing is worth roughly two orders of magnitude. That is more than enough to matter. Quoting the bigger number would be the numerical equivalent of the cherry-picked correlation you were warned about in Module 2 - technically true, and chosen because it flatters.
Never loop over a NumPy array in Python. If you must loop, loop over a list. If you can vectorize, do that instead and the question disappears.

And when you see a benchmark, ask what the baseline was. A speedup figure is a ratio, and ratios can be inflated by making the denominator worse rather than the numerator better. Usually that is someone benchmarking the thing that was convenient rather than the thing that was fair.

Python is a flexible language, and flexibility costs. Every time that loop touches an element, Python has to check what type it is, look up the right division routine, allocate a new object for the result, and add it to a growing list. A million values means a million rounds of that overhead.

NumPy stores its data in one solid block of memory, all of one type, and hands the arithmetic to compiled C code that loops without any of the per-element checking. You pay the flexibility cost once, when you build the array, instead of on every operation.
That is also why an array cannot hold mixed types, which will look like a limitation in section 3 and is actually the whole trick.
The name for what you just did is vectorization : expressing an operation on a whole array rather than on individual elements. It's shorter to write, and the speed comes free.

A Python list can hold anything. An array holds one type , recorded in its dtype , and that restriction is what makes the whole thing fast.

Integer arrays have no way to represent a missing value. There is no bit pattern for "absent" in an integer, so NumPy refuses:

The standard fix is to rescale each measure onto a common 0-to-1 range before combining them. For a single measure that is (x - x.min()) / (x.max() - x.min()) , which subtracts one number from an entire array and then divides an entire array by another number. Applied to all three measures at once, it subtracts three numbers, one per column, from a ten-row table.

Neither of those is an operation between equal-sized things. Both work anyway. The rule that makes them work is called broadcasting , and it is the part of NumPy that most repays understanding properly. Get it right and array code reads almost exactly like the formula it implements. Get it wrong and you meet ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together , which is the error you will see more than any other whi

You have in fact already relied on broadcasting three times in this notebook without it being named. This section names it. It starts with the easy case where shapes match exactly, shows what NumPy does when they do not, states the rule precisely, and then applies it to the cohort.
Two arrays of the same shape combine position by position.
a = np. array ([ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]) b = np. array ([ 10 , 20 , 30 , 40 ]) print (a + b) print (b - a) print (a * b) print (b / a)
Note a * b : that's [1*10, 2*20, ...] , not matrix multiplication. NumPy's * is element-wise. Matrix multiplication is @ , which you will not need in this course but should recognize.
All the comparison operators work element-wise too, and return an array of booleans:
print (a > 2 ) print (b == 20 )
Hold onto that - an array of booleans is how you filter data, in section 8.
So what happens when the shapes don't match?
The single number was applied to all six elements. NumPy did not build a 2-by-3 array of tens - it just reused the value, which costs nothing.
row = np. array ([ 10 , 20 , 30 ]) print ( f"M.shape = {M.shape}" ) print ( f"row.shape = {row.shape}" ) print () print (M + row)
The row was reused for each of the two rows of M . Column 0 got 10 , column 1 got 20 , column 2 got 30 .
The rule. Compare the shapes from the right. Two dimensions are compatible if they are equal, or if one of them is 1 :
M ( 2 , 3 ) row ( 3 ,) -> the 3 s match, and M's leading 2 is free result ( 2 , 3 )
And when they aren't compatible, NumPy refuses:
M + np. array ([ 10 , 20 ])
A ValueError , and the message is one to memorize: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,3) (2,) .
Reading right to left: 3 against 2 . Not equal, neither is 1 , so there is no way to line them up. NumPy will not guess.

You might reasonably have expected this to work - M has two rows and the array has two elements, so surely one per row? That is a natural thought and it is wrong, because broadcasting aligns from the right , not the left. To get the per-row behavior you have to say so explicitly:
col = np. array ([ 10 , 20 ]). reshape ( 2 , 1 ) # an explicit column print ( f"col.shape = {col.shape}" ) print (col) print () print (M + col)
Now the shapes are (2, 3) and (2, 1) . Right to left: 3 against 1 - one of them is 1, so it stretches. Then 2 against 2 - equal. Compatible.
np.newaxis does the same job and reads more clearly once you're used to it:
col = np. array ([ 10 , 20 ])[:, np.newaxis] print (col.shape) # np.newaxis IS None -- these three are the same thing print (np.newaxis is None ) print (np. array ([ 10 , 20 ])[:, None ].shape)

np.newaxis and None are literally the same object, so a[:, None] and a[:, np.newaxis] are identical. You will see both in the wild: np.newaxis is more self-documenting, [:, None] is shorter and very common in library source code and on Stack Overflow. Learn to read both.
When you get a broadcast ValueError, print both shapes and line them up from the right. The fix is almost always to reshape one operand so the dimensions align the way you meant.
The error message already contains both shapes. Read it instead of guessing.

Lee wants an engagement index that combines logins, hours, and submission rate. Those three are on completely different scales - logins run 4 to 17, hours run 2.0 to 12.4, submission is 0.61 to 1.00. Averaging them directly would let logins dominate purely because its numbers are bigger.
The fix is to normalize each measure to a 0-to-1 range first:
$$\text{normalized} = \frac{x - \min(x)}{\max(x) - \min(x)}$$
Here it is on one measure. Every operation below is broadcasting a single number across a 10-element array:
norm_logins = (logins - logins. min ()) / (logins. max () - logins. min ()) print (np. round (norm_logins, 3 )) print ( f"min {norm_logins.min()}, max {norm_logins.max()}" )
The lowest value maps to 0, the highest to 1, everything else in between. No loop, three operations, and it reads almost exactly like the formula.
You will do this for all three measures at once in the final challenge, using axis from section 11. That's the engagement index.
Three things are worth carrying out of this section.
The rule. Compare shapes from the right. Two dimensions are compatible when they are equal, or when one of them is 1. Nothing else is compatible, and NumPy will not guess on your behalf.

The direction. Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, not the left, which is why a 2-by-3 array and a 2-element array refuse to combine even though "2" appears in both. When you want per-row behavior you have to ask for it, either by reshaping to a column or by inserting an axis with np.newaxis . Why it matters beyond convenience. Broadcasting is what lets a formula written for one value apply unchanged to a whole table. Code like that expresses the idea instead of burying it in bookkeeping.

In Module 2 you learned that backup = scores does not copy a list - both names refer to the same object. Arrays have that behavior too, and one more : slicing an array does not copy either.

original = np. arange ( 6 ) print ( f"original: {original}" ) sub = original[ 2 : 4 ] print ( f"sub: {sub}" ) sub[ 0 ] = 99 print () print ( f"sub is now: {sub}" ) print ( f"original is now: {original}" )
original changed to [0 1 99 3 4 5] .
sub is a view - a window onto the same memory, not a new array. Writing through the window writes to the original.
This differs from lists, and the difference is easy to miss:
lst = [ 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 ] part = lst[ 1 : 3 ] # a COPY. changing part leaves lst alone arr = np. arange ( 4 ) part = arr[ 1 : 3 ] # a VIEW. changing part changes arr

NumPy works this way on purpose. Slicing a million-row array without copying it is instant and free; copying would cost time and memory every time you looked at a subset. The default is the one that scales.
When you genuinely want independent data, ask for it:
original = np. arange ( 6 ) safe = original[ 2 : 4 ]. copy () safe[ 0 ] = 99 print ( f"safe: {safe}" ) print ( f"original: {original}" )
np.may_share_memory will tell you which situation you're in, and it's a useful debugging tool:
a = np. arange ( 6 ) print (np. may_share_memory (a, a[ 2 : 4 ])) # a view print (np. may_share_memory (a, a[ 2 : 4 ]. copy ())) # a copy
Slicing an array gives a view. Slicing a list gives a copy.
If you are about to modify a subset and you need the original intact, call .copy() . If you're only reading, take the view - it's free.

Binary ufuncs take two arrays and combine them element-wise:

print (grad_gpa) print (grad_gpa + 1 )
nan stayed nan . That's the defining property: ** nan propagates.** Any arithmetic touching it produces nan , which means one missing value can silently poison an entire calculation.
print (grad_gpa. mean ())
nan . Not the mean of the nine real values - nan .
This is exactly right and completely unhelpful. NumPy is refusing to guess what the missing value should have been, which is honest, but it means your summary statistic is now unusable.

Note also that this is a silent failure in the sense that matters: no error, no warning, just a result that is wrong if you don't look at it. If a report prints nan you'll notice. If it feeds into another calculation first, you may not.
NumPy provides nan -aware versions of the aggregates, which skip missing values:

np.isnan gives a mask, so ~np.isnan(x) is the mask of values that are present. That's the connection back to section 8.
** nan is not zero and it is not an error - it propagates.**

np.nanmean and friends skip missing values, which is convenient and is also a decision you are making on the analyst's behalf. Dropping the missing value here means the graduate GPA average describes only students who have finished. That may be exactly right, or it may bias the number - and either way it belongs in the caveats, not buried in a function name.

std has a parameter, ddof , that decides what you divide by. NumPy defaults to ddof=0 - the population standard deviation, dividing by n. pandas defaults to ddof=1 - the sample standard deviation, dividing by n-1.

ppandas has a small vocabulary and uses it precisely. Its error messages assume you know these, and so does every answer you will find online. You don't have to have these memorized right now, but by the end of the module, you should know them. (Try using the flash card tool!)
Series - A one-dimensional array with an index. One column of a table, with labels attached to the values.
DataFrame - A set of Series sharing one index. The table, and the object most pandas work is about.
index - The labels attached to a DataFrame's rows. Identifiers, not positions - which is why .loc and .iloc differ.
.loc - Selection by label . df.loc[1003] asks for the row whose index is 1003, and includes the endpoint when slicing.
.iloc - Selection by integer position . df.iloc[0] asks for the first row, whatever its label.
dtype - The type of a column. object almost always means text got into something you expected to be numeric.
NaN - Not a Number: pandas' marker for a missing value. It is a float, and it propagates through arithmetic.
missing at random - When whether a value is missing has nothing to do with the outcome. If it is not true, dropping rows biases the answer.
boolean mask - A Series of True / False used to filter rows. Combine with & and | , never and and or .
groupby - Split rows into groups, apply a summary to each, combine the results. The dictionary-counting pattern, industrialized.
aggregation - The summary applied to each group - mean , count , median . Named aggregation gives the output readable column names.
merge - Joining two tables on a shared key. Check the key is unique first: a repeated key multiplies rows.
inner join - Keeps only rows present in both tables. Rows without a match are dropped silently, so check the row count.
left join - Keeps every row of the left table, filling gaps with NaN . Makes a missing match visible instead of absent.
pivot table - A groupby arranged as a grid: one variable down the side, another across the top, a statistic in the cells.
chained assignment - Writing df[mask]["col"] = x . It edits a temporary copy and silently does nothing. Use df.loc[mask, "col"] = x .
target leakage - Letting information about the outcome into a predictor. The model looks excellent in testing and fails in use.

That is the problem pandas exists to solve. It attaches labels to data and then refuses to let them come apart. Think of it as moving from using a calculator to a spreadsheet.

Nothing failed. No exception, no warning, no obviously wrong number - Priya plausibly could log in 3.4 times a week. This is the most dangerous class of bug in data work: the kind that produces a publishable-looking answer.
The fix is not "be careful." The fix is a data structure that carries the label with the value.

df = pd. DataFrame ({ "name" : [ "Amaka Okoroha" , "Devin Castellanos" , "Priya Raghunathan" ], "ug_gpa" : [ 3.02 , 1.99 , 2.80 ], "logins" : [ 3.4 , 0.4 , 4.4 ], }) df. sort_values ( "ug_gpa" , ascending= False )
One sort, every column moves together. The row is the unit, not the array.
That is the whole reason for pandas. Everything else - the selection syntax, the grouping, the merging - is built on the fact that a label and its values cannot be separated by accident.

There is a cost, though. NumPy has one way to index. pandas has three, they look almost identical, and two of them will do something you did not intend at least once each. Section 3 is about that, and it is the section you'll need spend extra time in, even if the rest makes sense.
pandas has two objects you need. Everything else is a method on one of them.
A Series is a one-dimensional array with an index. Think of one column in a table.
A DataFrame is a set of Series sharing one index. Think of the whole table.

That ambiguity is why .loc and .iloc exist, as you'll see in Section 3.

Both fail, and the two error types tell you which question you asked.

Read those two words as the question you asked. KeyError means "no such label." IndexError means "no such position."

Generally, you want to use .loc . Position is typically meaningless, and frequently changes. A label is meaningful - if you make it so. Code written with .loc keeps meaning the same thing after a sort_values , and code written with .iloc does not.
Both take a row selector and a column selector, separated by a comma.

.loc[a:b] includes b . .iloc[a:b] excludes it, like every other slice in Python.

One caution about label slices

That worked cleanly because the index is sorted . A label slice does not sort - it finds where a sits, finds where b sits, and takes everything between them in the order the rows happen to be stored .

Devin (1089) is inside a slice that reads 1003:1024 , even though 1089 is larger than 1024.

Nothing is broken. The slice took every row between the position of 1003 and the position of 1024, and on this ordering Devin sits between them. On a sorted index that is the same thing as "every label in the range." On an unsorted one it is not.

Three reasons, in increasing order of importance:
It does not usually save memory. pandas generally builds the new object anyway and then rebinds the name, so the promised efficiency mostly is not real.
It returns None , which breaks more complex method usage. df.drop_duplicates(inplace=True).head() is an AttributeError , and the message will not mention inplace .

It changes an object you cannot see. In a notebook, cells run in whatever order you click them. **A % or a $ or a comma in a number column silently makes it text.**
Nothing is wrong here. A human reading 84% sees a number. pandas sees a five-character string, and every mathematical method on the column is disabled from the moment the file is read.
This is why .info() is the first thing you run. The dtype tells you before you waste an hour on a calculation that cannot work.
The string methods you learned in Module 2 work on a whole column through .str . names.str.strip().str.title() cleans every value at once, no loop required.

These are pandas' own versions of those methods rather than Python's, and the difference shows up on missing data. A list comprehension calling .upper() on a column with a blank in it raises AttributeError . .str.upper() leaves the blank alone and keeps going. This is Module 3's vectorization, applied to text.

matplotlib's vocabulary is small and its error messages assume you know it. The first four entries in particular are worth learning early, because almost every question you ask online will be answered in those words.
Figure - The whole image. It owns the figure-level title, the size, and saving to a file.
Axes - One plot inside a Figure. It owns the data, the labels, the legend, and the two axis objects. An Axes is not an axis.
Axis - A single scale on an Axes, with its ticks, limits and formatting.
Artist - Anything matplotlib draws. Every line, dot, label and spine is one.
explicit interface - Creating fig, ax and calling methods on them. Also called the object-oriented interface, and the only one this course uses.
implicit interface - The plt.plot style, which adds to whatever Axes matplotlib thinks is current. Convenient for one throwaway chart, and the reason a second chart lands in the wrong place.
constrained layout - The layout engine requested with layout="constrained" , which sizes the gaps so labels do not collide. It replaces tight_layout , and calling tight_layout() switches it off.
bin - One interval a histogram counts values into. The bin count is a choice you make, and it changes the shape the reader sees.
alpha - Opacity, from 0 to 1. Below 1, overlapping points look darker than single ones, which is how a scatter plot admits that two students landed in the same place.
colormap - The mapping from a number to a color. Sequential for ordered values, diverging for a meaningful middle, qualitative for unordered categories.
perceptually uniform - A colormap in which equal steps in the data look like equal steps in color. viridis is; jet is not, which is why it invents boundaries the data does not have.
colorbar - The key for a colormap. Ask the Figure for it: fig.colorbar(mappable, ax=ax) .
relative luminance - How bright a color is, and therefore what gray it prints as. Two colors of similar luminance are the same color to a monochrome printer.
small multiples - A grid of panels sharing a scale, so several comparisons can be read at once. sharey=True is what makes them comparable.
dpi - Dots per inch when a figure is saved as a raster image. 72 is a thumbnail, 150 a document figure, 300 print.
raster and vector - Raster formats (PNG) store pixels and blur when enlarged. Vector formats (PDF, SVG) store drawing instructions and do not.
axes-level function - A seaborn function that draws onto an Axes you pass with ax= , such as histplot or regplot .
figure-level function - A seaborn function that builds its own figure and cannot take ax= , such as pairplot or displot . Customize it through the grid object it returns.
truncated axis - A value axis that does not start at zero. On a bar chart, where the reader compares lengths, it misrepresents the comparison.
confounder - A third variable that produces an apparent relationship between two others. Faceting or coloring by it is the visual control.

Three things a figure is for
From the course lecture, and worth keeping in this order, because it is also the order the capstone runs in:
what is in here that I did not expect?
here is what I found, and why I believe it
here is what we should do about it
The same numbers can serve all three, and the figure that serves one badly serves the others worse. An exploratory chart is allowed to be ugly and fast. A chart in a Cabinet report is not.
Which chart answers which question
Choosing a chart type by how it looks, rather than by the structure of the data and the question being asked, is how a figure ends up unreadable. Each type has a job:
the shape of a distribution: skew, spread, whether there is one hump or two
comparing distributions across categories
median, quartiles and outliers, compactly enough to line several up
relationship, clusters and outliers. Color or size can carry a third variable
comparing discrete categories
one value per category, compared by length. Start the axis at zero
change over an ordered variable, usually time
trend and continuity. The line claims the values between the points exist
which variables move together, most often a correlation matrix

Three to be wary of, all of which section 9 takes apart: pie charts , because comparing angles is harder than comparing lengths; three-dimensional charts , where the depth carries no data and distorts the comparison; and dual-axis charts , which let the person drawing them decide how related two series appear.

An Axes means a single set of axes, which is one panel of the figure, while an axis is one scale on it. The two words look like a singular and a plural of each other, which is what makes the naming confusing the first time and clear after that.
The practical rule: if it is about the picture, ask the Figure. If it is about the data, ask the Axes.

The other interface, once
matplotlib has a second way to draw the same figure, and you will meet it constantly, so it is worth seeing exactly once.

The implicit interface, also called the pyplot interface, keeps track of the last figure and axes you touched and adds things to whatever it thinks you meant. The explicit interface, the one this module uses, hands you the objects and makes you name them.
Here is one figure, drawn both ways.
# implicit: no objects are named, and there is no way to refer back plt. plot ([ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]) plt. ylabel ( "some numbers" ) plt. show ()
# explicit: the same figure, with the objects named fig, ax = plt. subplots () ax. plot ([ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]) ax. set_ylabel ( "some numbers" ) plt. show ()
Identical output, four lines each. On one plot the difference is preference. Here is where it stops being preference.
plt. plot ([ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]) plt. plot ([ 100 , 200 , 300 , 400 ]) plt. plot ([ 1000 , 2000 , 3000 , 4000 ]) plt. ylabel ( "some numbers" ) plt. show ()

All three landed on the same Axes, because that is what the implicit interface is for: it adds to the current one. The first series is now a flat line at the bottom, unreadable, because it shares a y axis with values a thousand times larger. Nothing failed. You just cannot see two thirds of your data.

# The explicit fix: three Axes, named, each with its own scale. fig, axes = plt. subplots ( 3 , 1 , figsize=( 5.5 , 5 ), layout= "constrained" ) series = [[ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ], [ 100 , 200 , 300 , 400 ], [ 1000 , 2000 , 3000 , 4000 ]] for ax, values in zip (axes, series): ax. plot (values) ax. set_ylabel ( "numbers" ) axes[- 1 ]. set_xlabel ( "index" ) fig. suptitle ( "Three scales, three Axes" ) plt. show ()
You will need to read the implicit form, because most examples online use it. The mapping is nearly mechanical:
ax.set_xticks(pos, labels)
The pattern: a plt. function that sets something becomes ax.set_something . A plt. function that draws something keeps its name and moves onto the Axes.

The first question about any column is what its values do: where they sit, how far they range, whether they cluster in one place or two. The histogram answers it by counting values into bins and drawing the counts.
That word bins is doing more work than it looks.

At 5 bins the tallest bar holds 37 of the 100 students, and the distribution looks like one solid block. At 25 bins the tallest holds 10, one bin is empty, and the same data looks ragged and possibly bumpy. Nothing about the students changed between those three pictures. The bin width is a choice you made, and it is a choice your reader cannot see.
Choosing a bin count honestly
There is no correct number, which is exactly why it has to be a deliberate choice rather than a default you never looked at.
Too few bins and real structure disappears into one block.
Too many and sampling noise looks like structure.
Look at two or three before you settle, which is what you just did.
matplotlib will also compute a bin count for you from the data, using rules that account for both the spread and the sample size.
for rule in [ "auto" , "sturges" , "fd" ]: edges = np. histogram_bin_edges (scores. dropna (), bins=rule) print ( f"{rule:8} -> {len(edges) - 1} bins, width {edges[1] - edges[0]:.1f}" )

Report the bin count, or use a named rule and say which. A histogram without that information cannot be reproduced, and the reader has no way to know whether the shape is in the data or in your choice.

A boxplot throws away the shape and keeps the summary: median, the middle half, the reach of the whiskers, and anything beyond them drawn as a point.

Note tick_labels= in that call. It used to be labels= , which was removed from matplotlib in version 3.11. If you find an example online using labels= on a boxplot, that is the version you are looking at, not a mistake in your code.

The boxplot is compact and exact about the quartiles, and it is blind to shape. A distribution with two separate humps and a distribution with one can produce very similar boxes. Use the box when you are comparing several groups at once and the shape is not the point. Use the histogram when it is.

Histogram for shape, boxplot for comparison. The boxplot's advantage appears the moment you have four groups to line up, which is section 5. Its cost is that it hides everything the shape would have told you.

A fitted line summarizes the trend. It is worth adding when the reader needs the direction and rough rate. It is worth being careful about, because a line invites two readings it does not support.

What the line says: across these 85 students, each additional login per week goes with about 4 more points on average.

Error bars, and saying what they are

An error bar is the usual fix for a bar chart that hides its spread. It is only useful if the reader knows what the bar represents, because a standard deviation and a standard error of the mean differ by a factor of the square root of n and look identical on the page.

Always label what the error bar is. Standard deviation describes the students; standard error describes how well the mean is pinned down, and it shrinks as the sample grows. A reader who assumes the wrong one will read the wrong amount of certainty off your figure.

The three checks, in the order they are worth running:
Design. Is anything on this figure not helping it say its sentence?

Data. Does the axis start where the comparison requires? Is this every observation, or a filtered subset? Did I choose the bins, the bands, or the split point after seeing what they did to the picture?

Color is the fastest channel a figure has and the easiest one to misuse. Two questions decide almost every color choice: what kind of variable is being encoded, and who has to read the result.
Four kinds of colormap, four kinds of question
matplotlib groups its colormaps into four classes, and the class is chosen by the data rather than by taste:
the value has an order and one end matters
there is a meaningful middle, and both directions matter
the value wraps around, like an angle or time of day
the categories have no order at all
The mistake this taxonomy prevents is using a qualitative palette for an ordered variable, which tells the reader the categories are unrelated when they are a sequence.

A version control system records every change you make to your files over time, so you can go back to any earlier state of your project. Think of it as an unlimited undo history - not just for one file, but for your entire project directory.

For data scientists, this matters because your work is rarely linear. You'll try an approach, hit a dead end, and need to backtrack. You'll share a notebook with a teammate who changes it in ways that break your analysis. You'll want to know exactly what changed between the version that worked and the version that didn't. Version control handles all of this.
Git is the most widely used version control system in the world. GitHub is a hosting platform built on top of Git that adds collaboration features like pull requests, code review, and issue tracking.

Git is a command-line tool - you interact with it by typing commands into a text window called a terminal , not by clicking through a graphical interface. Most developers prefer this because it's faster, scriptable, and it's exactly how Git is used in professional environments.
The terminal runs a program called a shell that interprets your commands. The shell you'll use depends on your operating system:
macOS ships with the Terminal app running zsh. You can also use iTerm2 as a more feature-rich alternative. All commands in this course work on Mac Terminal.
Windows uses PowerShell or CMD by default, but Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows) gives you a Bash shell that uses the same commands as Mac and Linux.

Before diving into the states, it helps to know how Git stores your work. Unlike tools that track a list of changes ("line 14 changed from X to Y"), Git saves a complete snapshot of every file in your project each time you commit - like taking a photograph of the entire folder at that moment. This is why reverting to any point in history is instant: Git just loads the snapshot from that commit rather than replaying a

This snapshot model is also why git add and git commit are two separate steps. You're first choosing what goes into the snapshot (staging), then pressing the shutter (committing). Every file in a Git project lives in one of three states that reflect where it is in that process:
Your actual files on disk. When you edit a notebook or Python script, the changes live here until you stage them.
A holding zone for changes you're about to commit. You choose which changes to include - not every edit has to go into the same commit.
The committed history. Once changes are committed, Git permanently records a snapshot. This is your undo history.
A copy of your repository hosted on GitHub. Push to share your commits with others; pull to receive theirs.
Almost every Git session follows the same pattern. Once you have a repository set up, the day-to-day cycle looks like this:

# 1. Pull in any changes your teammates made git pull origin main # 2. Make changes to your files (edit, add, delete) # 3. Stage the changes you want to include git add analysis.py # stage one file git add . # stage everything # 4. Commit with a descriptive message git commit -m "Add batting average normalization step" # 5. Push your commits to GitHub git push origin main

Write commit messages as if you're finishing the sentence "This commit will..." - so "Add batting average normalization step" rather than "stuff" or "fixed it". Your future self will thank you when you're scrolling through history three months later.
There are three common ways to start a Git project depending on your situation: initialize a brand new one locally, clone an existing one from GitHub, or fork someone else's repo and clone your copy.
Option A: Start locally (local-first)
Use this when you're starting a brand new project from scratch on your own machine. You create the folder, initialize Git, make your first commit, then connect it to GitHub.

# 1. Create a folder and navigate into it mkdir my-project cd my-project # 2. Initialize Git git init # 3. Add files and make your first commit git add . git commit -m "Initial commit" # 4. Connect to a GitHub repo you already created on github.com git remote add origin https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git git push -u origin main
Option B: Start from GitHub (remote-first)

Use this when the repo already exists on GitHub - either one you created there, or one your instructor set up. git clone downloads the entire repo, history and all, and wires up the remote automatically.
# Clone creates the folder for you git clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git cd your-repo # You're ready to work - remote is already configured git remote -v # verify the remote is set
Option C: Fork then clone (course workflow)

Forking creates your own independent copy of someone else's repository under your GitHub account. You can push changes to your fork freely without affecting the original. This is the standard workflow for course assignments and open-source contributions.
The steps are always the same:
1. On GitHub, open the repo you want to work with and click the Fork button (top right). GitHub creates a copy at github.com/your-username/repo-name .
2. Clone your fork (not the original) to your machine:
git clone https://github.com/your-username/repo-name.git cd repo-name
Any commits you push go to your fork. If you want to propose changes back to the original, you open a pull request from your fork - the same PR workflow covered in the Pull Requests section below.
A common mistake: cloning the original repo instead of your fork. If you do that, you won't have push access. Always copy the URL from your forked version of the repo on GitHub.

A branch is an independent copy of your project history that you can work on without touching the main codebase. When you're building a new feature, fixing a bug, or running an experiment, you do that work on a branch. If it goes well, you merge it back. If it doesn't, you discard the branch and nothing is lost.

# See all branches (the * marks your current branch) git branch # Create a new branch and switch to it git checkout -b feature/add-salary-viz # Do your work, commit as normal, then push the branch git push origin feature/add-salary-viz # Switch back to main git checkout main
The convention is to keep main always in a working, deployable state. All active development happens on branches. This is how professional teams prevent broken code from reaching the shared codebase.

When your branch is ready, you merge it back into main. Git will try to combine the changes automatically. If two branches modified the same lines of the same file, Git cannot decide which version is correct - that's a merge conflict .

# Merge a branch into main git checkout main git merge feature/add-salary-viz # If a conflict occurs, Git marks the file: # # your version of the code # ======= # the incoming version # >>>>>>> feature/add-salary-viz # Edit the file to resolve, then: git add analysis.py git commit -m "Merge salary viz feature, resolve conflict"

Merge conflicts are a normal part of collaborative work - not a sign something went wrong. Git is simply telling you it needs a human to decide which version of the code is correct. Read both sides carefully before choosing.

On GitHub, you don't usually merge branches directly from the command line when working on a team. Instead, you open a Pull Request (PR) - a proposal to merge your branch into main, with a built-in discussion thread for code review.
The pull request workflow looks like this:

Push your branch to GitHub, then open a PR through the GitHub interface. A teammate reviews your changes, leaves comments, and either approves or requests changes. Once approved, the branch is merged and you delete the branch to keep the repo clean.
Always git pull before you start new work. Write clear commit messages. Use branches for every new feature or fix. Review your own PR before asking someone else to. Delete merged branches.
